post1.text:
Most companies don't stall at $50M because of bad strategy. They stall because leadership didn't scale with the business.

Recent moves by fast-growing companies in energy and AI show a consistent pattern: the moment they commit to serious scaling, the first thing they restructure is the executive team. Not the product. Not the go-to-market. The people at the top.

Here is what that tells leaders running $50M-plus organizations:

1. The skills that got you to $50M are not the skills that carry you to $500M. This is uncomfortable and it is also non-negotiable.

2. Leadership gaps compound faster than revenue gaps. A weak executive layer slows every function below it.

3. Scaling is not a growth problem. It is a leadership capacity problem wearing a growth problem's clothes.

The companies that reach $500M don't find better markets. They build leadership teams that can actually operate at that altitude.

What is the one leadership gap in your organization that nobody is talking about out loud?

post2.text:
A recent piece in citybiz covered CleanCapital's decision to reshape its entire executive team as it scales its solar and storage platform. Worth reading for one specific reason: they didn't wait for the cracks to show.

At Autobahn, we see this constantly with companies pushing from $50M toward $500M. The leaders who scale successfully restructure the team before the pressure forces them to. The ones who wait restructure in crisis mode, and that is a far more expensive lesson.

If you are scaling a business right now, the question isn't whether your leadership team needs to evolve. It's whether you are willing to act on that before it becomes urgent.

Read the full article here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMisAFBVV95cUxNWWJYVV83U0lvX2xxQWtKRUtiVE1lUERRd1pEN2MyU1BodHItU2tJVzJyOV9mSXRjM0M1TFhMMjdYamFoWDVYU2Nwdy1iQjRTSjFqR0FfWWdLNGRqZTBFbFJBUkxtQ21GLWQ1V082elZrcV8wV2ZjZ3VkM3lSSUdMM2ZDSUtqVnZaQ0R1anpQMllSU1JLUk1tWE01dENROWlSQlJNNk1lUkVJcmZLbWZkZQ?oc=5

post3.text:
When CleanCapital restructured its executive team to support serious growth, they were doing something Katherine Slain writes about directly in Chapter 1 of Rock Your Business.

The chapter is called Lead Like Lives Depend On It. The title is not a metaphor.

Katherine's core argument is that leadership at scale carries a different kind of weight. The decisions made at the top of a $50M-plus company affect jobs, families, communities, and futures in ways most leaders haven't fully reckoned with. When you understand that, the way you build and evaluate your leadership team changes completely.

Most books tell you to hire well. This chapter tells you why the stakes are higher than you think and what that actually demands of you.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
Most founders optimize for revenue. The ones who actually build wealth optimize for multiple.

Those are not the same thing, and confusing them is one of the most expensive mistakes we see at the $50M to $500M stage.

A recent Entrepreneur piece made this point sharply: founders pour years into growth, then arrive at the exit table without ever having engineered what the business looks like to a buyer. The result is a lower multiple, a longer deal process, or a deal that never closes.

Here is what changes when you think like a seller years before you sell:

1. Revenue quality matters more than revenue volume. Recurring, contracted, and diversified revenue commands a premium. Lumpy, customer-concentrated revenue gets discounted hard.

2. EBITDA margin tells the story a buyer actually reads. Top-line growth with thin margins signals a business that needs the buyer more than the buyer needs it.

3. Management depth is a multiplier. If the business cannot run without the founder for 90 days, buyers price in that risk.

If you sold your company today, would the multiple reflect what you have actually built?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Forbes on exit planning lays out the foundational elements every business owner should have in place before a transaction, and it is worth a read for any leader in the $50M to $500M range.

What the article gets right: exit planning is not an event. It is a discipline that should be running in the background years before you are ready to sell.

What we would add from our work with scaling companies: the gap between what founders think their business is worth and what the market will actually pay is almost always wider than expected. Closing that gap takes time, intentional structuring, and often a complete rethink of how value is documented and presented.

Start earlier than you think you need to. The founders who do are the ones who walk away satisfied.

Read the full article here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiogFBVV95cUxPQjFIYXhibGVtZGsyVmtwMGZpTjdobTVlcEJOMURid0JybUZzRjlzc212dU85c29LdEFYMXJDRU1vNzYtVXZIZzFhZVU0T3RpdzZ5VnR2bkZ2ZXJPRG83d1hiTFJ4UF85WHR5QnNJc0wzdEdqS0xsQXdFVi1JeG0zSGxYY3ZtX1ZUYkxWaDRpcE9sTENEVlNuN1pKTkxzZmRyOGc

post3.text:
Exit planning articles are everywhere right now, and most of them stop at the obvious: get your financials clean, know your EBITDA, find an advisor.

Chapter 2 of Rock Your Business goes further.

Titled "Maximize Your Multiple to Achieve Your Exit," and authored by Paul Belair and George Hohman, this chapter is built for founders and CEOs who are running companies in the $50M to $500M range and want to understand how buyers actually assign value, not just how sellers hope they do.

One thing the chapter makes clear: the multiple a buyer offers is not primarily a reward for past performance. It is a bet on future risk. Knowing how to reduce perceived risk in the eyes of a buyer is a skill, and it can be developed well before you are ready to sell.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

The multiple you receive is not a verdict on your effort. It is a calculation buyers make about risk, revenue quality, and whether the business can survive without you. Here is what the most successful exits have in common.

post1.text:
Most strategic plans fail not because the strategy was wrong, but because execution was never actually designed.

Leadership teams spend weeks in offsite meetings building beautiful plans, then hand them to managers who have no idea how to translate a slide deck into daily decisions. Forbes recently highlighted how this gap between strategy and execution is the primary reason leadership teams underperform, and it has nothing to do with intelligence or effort.

Here is what $50M+ leaders need to hear:

1. Strategy without an execution owner is just a document. Every strategic priority needs a named accountable person, not a committee.

2. Your quarterly rhythm matters more than your annual plan. Companies that review progress every 90 days catch drift before it becomes damage.

3. Improvisation is not failure. Markets shift. The companies that scale well build plans that are directionally firm but tactically flexible.

The strategy is not the work. Getting your team to actually do the work, consistently, in the right direction, is the work.

What is the single biggest gap between your strategy and your execution right now?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Forbes breaks down exactly why leadership teams fail at strategy execution, and the findings are worth sitting with if you are running a company between $50M and $500M.

The core problem is not bad strategy. It is the absence of systems that connect strategy to the daily work people actually do. At that growth stage, the informal coordination that worked at $10M stops working entirely. You need structure, and most leaders underestimate how much structure is required.

At Autobahn Consultants, we see this constantly. The companies that scale successfully are not the ones with the best strategies. They are the ones that build disciplined execution habits before they feel like they need them.

Read the full piece and ask yourself honestly where the gap lives in your organization.

Bridging strategy and execution is one of the defining challenges for companies scaling past $50M. It is also one of the most practical chapters in our upcoming book.

Chapter 3 of Rock Your Business, titled "What We Learned Selling Fish Food and Nike Shoes," was written by Rafa Loyo and Jim Randall. Their background spans industries that look nothing alike on the surface, and that is exactly the point. The strategic planning lessons they draw out apply whether you are moving inventory or managing complex service engagements.

One thing Rafa and Jim make clear: the companies that execute well are not the ones with the most sophisticated plans. They are the ones that know how to simplify a plan until every person on the team can actually act on it.

There is a framework in this chapter that will change how you run your next planning cycle. We will let the book do the talking.

post1.text:
Most companies at $50M think they have a sales strategy. They don't. They have a sales habit.

There's a difference. A habit is what your team does because it worked before. A strategy is a deliberate system designed to win specific customers in specific markets at a specific margin. McKinsey's latest research on B2B growth confirms what we see inside scaling companies every day: the gap between top performers and everyone else isn't talent or product. It's whether the business treats revenue growth as a managed discipline or a happy accident.

Three things leaders at this stage consistently get wrong:

1. They confuse pipeline volume with pipeline quality. More leads is not a strategy.
2. They let their best salespeople define the process instead of the other way around.
3. They have no written ideal customer profile, so every deal feels winnable.

A real sales strategy tells you who to say no to just as clearly as it tells you who to pursue.

What would change in your business if your sales process ran the same way with or without your top rep?

post2.text:
A recent piece from abasto.com makes a point that scaling companies can't afford to ignore: B2B sales strategy now requires AI-driven personalization just to stay competitive, not to get ahead.

Here's what that actually means for a business between $50M and $500M. You can no longer treat every prospect the same way and expect the same results. Buyers have more information, shorter patience, and higher expectations than they did five years ago. Generic outreach is not just ineffective. It's a signal that you don't understand their business.

At Autobahn, we push our clients to stop selling to segments and start selling to situations. When you map your sales motion to what a specific buyer is actually experiencing, conversion improves and so does the quality of the relationship.

Read the full article and think about where your current approach falls short: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMikgFBVV95cUxNeXlWSGVIUEpjeTZGWVJQMzBJWU1DSl80Y3dVRkZ0eS05QjI3cWo4clgzNXFzRnh1eWp3VWN0T0FPQnl5TnNIcWw4RFVKUTZWSk5fTy1zSk5FSmNtOW80MmN1THVoNjRsZWVZVUNIRGR1UkQxWE9ZZWhGX1A0bkdzVk5BemNDV05DVDR5X2VFNHVXZw?oc=5

post3.text:
New McKinsey data on B2B growth confirms something Deb and Brandon write about directly in Chapter 4 of our upcoming book: every day your company operates without a real sales strategy is a day you are funding your own inefficiency.

That chapter title is not a metaphor. It is a calculation. When you have no defined sales strategy, you are spending real money on salespeople, tools, and time chasing the wrong customers at the wrong margins with no repeatable system to fix it.

What Deb and Brandon lay out is a way to diagnose whether what you call a sales strategy actually functions as one under pressure. Most leaders are surprised by what they find.

If your revenue growth depends more on who showed up to work today than on the system your team runs, this chapter was written for you.

post1.text:
Most companies at $50M think their marketing problem is a budget problem. It is not. It is an identity problem.

Ulta's CMO recently spoke about how the brand deliberately balances emotional connection with channel performance. The insight that stands out: the brands winning at scale are not spending more. They are being more intentional about what they stand for before they decide where to show up.

For leaders scaling past $50M, here is what that actually means in practice:

1. Your brand has a scent before you walk in the room. Customers are forming opinions based on your website, your sales team's language, and your LinkedIn presence long before a proposal is signed.

2. Consistency compounds. A fragmented brand identity across channels does not just confuse buyers. It slows your sales cycle and inflates your customer acquisition cost.

3. Brand is not marketing's job alone. It is a leadership decision that every department either reinforces or undermines every single day.

If your company doubled in revenue tomorrow, would your brand hold up under the pressure?

#Branding #ScalingBusiness #MarketingStrategy

post2.text:
A recent piece in Marketing Dive spotlighted how Ulta's CMO is threading the needle between long-term brand building and immediate omnichannel performance. It is a nuanced challenge most large retailers face, but the lesson applies directly to companies scaling from $50M toward $500M.

At Autobahn, we see this tension constantly. Leaders at this stage want attribution and awareness, ROI and reputation, all at once. The companies that scale well do not choose between brand and performance. They build systems where both inform each other.

The trap is treating brand as the soft, unmeasurable side of marketing. In reality, a clear brand identity is one of your highest-leverage growth tools, because it makes every other marketing dollar work harder.

If your marketing efforts feel disconnected, it may be time to audit what your brand is actually communicating. Read the full piece here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiogFBVV95cUxPRlFnSEozTXJJdnl5aWFJQTFGR0tkcnhrUnUyOTNZNlIwcHZiLWFnbm0tQ0FWZEZCTWZvdUFQeEFvQkIwOHdpMmZBR3I5WmNjRmFYb0xJMGhQWmJHYUdWUVdyWndOWTYwR1ZQQ2E4V1dMV2NrT0hpRzNaU1VKdUdoZHMwSFB4SlhYTkZKZ2hDdEdsSkJ6TW91UTZTWlNGaGVmcUE?oc=5

post3.text:
The conversation around brand building at Ulta, Eli Lilly, and the Cannes Lions shortlist all point to the same underlying truth: brand is a growth driver, not a decoration.

Chapter 5 of Rock Your Business, titled 'What Does Your Marketing Smell Like?' tackles this head on. Written by Kayli Simpson and Yasmin West, the chapter challenges leaders to think about brand the way customers actually experience it, not the way executives present it in board decks.

One of the sharpest ideas in the chapter is that your brand has an ambient quality. It is present even when you are not actively marketing. That invisible signal either attracts the right clients and talent, or it quietly repels them.

If you are scaling past $50M, this chapter will make you rethink what your company is actually putting into the air.

Rock Your Business, by Jonathan Slain and Katherine Slain, available soon. Follow us for updates.

Companies scaling past $50M often discover that their messaging, visuals, and customer experience are all saying slightly different things, and that friction is silently killing growth. post1.text:
Hiring more people is not a growth strategy. It is a cost center with a logo on it.

SHRM recently reported that the most effective hiring leaders in 2026 are shifting away from volume recruiting and toward precision targeting. Fewer roles, sharper definitions, higher standards. That shift matters enormously if you are running a company between $50M and $500M.

Here is what that actually looks like in practice:

First, your job architecture needs to be built before you post a single role. If your org chart is fuzzy, every hire you make reinforces the confusion.

Second, the cost of a wrong hire at this stage is not just salary. It is momentum. A bad hire in a senior seat can set a scaling company back 12 to 18 months.

Third, talent strategy should be tied directly to your three-year revenue plan. If your CHRO is not in the room when growth targets are set, you already have a misalignment problem.

Growth companies do not need more people. They need the right people in the right seats at the right time.

What is the one role at your company that, if filled perfectly, would change everything?

post2.text:
A recent piece in SHRM lays out a clear case: the era of spray-and-pray hiring is over. In 2026, the companies winning the talent game are hiring with precision, not volume. Smaller candidate pools, tighter role definitions, and sharper criteria for what success actually looks like in a seat.

For companies scaling past $50M, this is not a trend to watch. It is a pressure test happening right now.

At Autobahn, we see it consistently. Growth stalls not because of market conditions, but because the wrong people are in the wrong roles. Precision hiring is not just an HR function. It is an operational discipline.

If your hiring process was built for a $20M company, it will not get you to $200M.

Read the full SHRM piece and ask yourself whether your current talent approach is built for where you are going, not where you have been.

post3.text:
SHRM is calling it: precision hiring is replacing volume hiring as the dominant model for 2026 and beyond. That conclusion sits right at the center of Chapter 6 in our upcoming book, Rock Your Business.

Chapter 6 is called The Talent Engine. It was written by Caleb Hawkins, Darla Klein, and Yasmin West, and it is one of the most direct chapters in the book. No theory. No soft frameworks. Just a hard look at how scaling companies build the people infrastructure that can actually support growth from $50M to $500M.

One thing the chapter makes clear: talent is not a department. It is a system. And like any system, it either scales with you or it breaks under pressure.

The question every leader should be sitting with is whether their talent engine is built for the company they are becoming, not the one they already are.

Rock Your Business, by Jonathan Slain and Katherine Slain, available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
More KPIs do not make better leaders. They make paralyzed ones.

Most companies scaling past $50M fall into the same trap: they add metrics every quarter until the dashboard becomes noise. Nobody acts on the numbers because nobody agrees on which numbers matter.

Oracle NetSuite recently catalogued 30 financial metrics worth tracking in 2026. Thirty. That list is useful as a reference. It is a disaster as a management system.

Here is what we see in high-growth companies that actually perform:

First, the leadership team owns three to five metrics that directly connect to strategic priorities, not operational comfort.

Second, every KPI has a named owner and a defined cadence for review. A metric without accountability is just a number on a slide.

Third, when a metric stops driving decisions, it gets cut. Dashboards should shrink as clarity grows.

The goal is not measurement. The goal is behavior change.

How many KPIs does your leadership team genuinely act on versus simply report?

post2.text:
A recent piece in CLA Connect laid out the KPIs manufacturers should use to improve company performance. Solid tactical list covering throughput, utilization, and quality metrics.

Here is the angle that matters if you are scaling: knowing which KPIs to track and knowing which ones to prioritize for your specific growth stage are two completely different problems.

We work with companies pushing from $50M toward $500M. At that scale, the wrong metrics do not just mislead, they misalign entire leadership teams. People optimize for what gets measured, even when the measurement is pointing in the wrong direction.

If you are in manufacturing and serious about scaling, this article is worth your time. Then ask yourself whether your current KPIs are driving growth or just documenting activity.

Read it here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiugFBVV95cUxNc3hGVVVxVnMwVEpLcmxaNWJzaURJbERjczZaSDhlcnhvOFlHX1VZU0tETkctQjFqRVhZVkNtcFNoUWtfSmRhSmU5N3pYc25IVzlfTEs5TjFZWk1RTmhZd2JzSkpPSXVmQndRRHRBM29CaDBoWnVWRXcxMnBhWkcwT3dmWTAwSDFSeS1hYzFtRUNtd05nWE9PX25nbzRfc2ZzSjVFVURMY0hMRkdVMmtOdjVOYUluUXJIcEE

post3.text:
Oracle NetSuite recently published a list of 30 financial KPIs every business should consider tracking. It is a genuinely useful resource. It also illustrates exactly the problem our contributors tackle in Chapter 7 of our upcoming book.

Chapter 7 is called Death by KPIs. It was written by Hector Arias, Matt Radicelli, and Jim Randall, and it addresses something most scaling companies discover too late: there is a point where more measurement actively slows you down.

One insight the chapter surfaces is that KPI overload is rarely a data problem. It is a leadership alignment problem. The metrics multiplied because the priorities were never clear enough to constrain them.

If your team is drowning in dashboards, this chapter was written for you.

post1.text:
Buying AI tools is not an AI strategy. That distinction is costing companies millions.

A recent study found that nine out of ten executives say AI has not meaningfully improved productivity at their organizations. That number should stop every scaling company in its tracks. Not because AI is failing, but because deployment is.

Here is what leaders at the $50M to $500M stage need to understand:

First, AI returns compound on process maturity. If your workflows are fragmented, AI accelerates the mess, not the output.

Second, your team needs a designated space to experiment with AI without it threatening their job security. Fear kills adoption faster than any technical barrier.

Third, productivity gains from AI are almost never immediate. The leaders seeing real returns invested in a 90-day learning curve before measuring outcomes.

The companies winning with AI right now are not the ones with the biggest budgets. They are the ones with the clearest internal structures.

So the real question is: does your team have the environment and the permission to actually learn how to use these tools?

At Autobahn, we work with leaders who are scaling fast. The ones getting AI right are building structured adoption frameworks first, then measuring results. The ones struggling skipped that step.

Read the Fortune piece and then ask yourself where your company actually stands.

The leaders most qualified to scale a company are often the ones most convinced they are about to be exposed as frauds.

That is not a weakness. It is almost a prerequisite.

Forbes Australia recently explored why imposter syndrome does not fade as leaders climb higher. It intensifies. The stakes grow, the visibility grows, and so does the internal noise.

Here is what $50M+ leaders need to understand about that reality:

1. Self-doubt at scale is not a sign you are in the wrong seat. It is a sign you are paying attention to how much is on the line.

2. The leaders who perform best under pressure are not the ones who eliminated doubt. They are the ones who stopped waiting for it to disappear before making decisions.

3. If your leadership team never admits uncertainty, that is a culture problem, not a confidence problem. Psychological safety starts at the top.

The question is not whether you feel like an imposter. The question is whether you let that feeling make decisions for you.

What has helped you lead through the moments when your confidence and your competence were not aligned?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Bona Magazine takes on imposter syndrome from an angle worth pausing on: self-doubt, channeled correctly, can actually sharpen executive presence rather than erode it.

That framing matters a lot for companies in the $50M to $500M growth corridor.

At that stage, leadership teams are operating in territory they have never navigated before. The self-doubt is real because the problems are genuinely new. The mistake most leaders make is treating that doubt as disqualifying rather than informative.

At Autobahn, we work with executives who are highly capable and quietly terrified in equal measure. The ones who scale well learn to distinguish between doubt that signals a real gap and doubt that is just noise.

If your leadership team is growing faster than its confidence, that is worth a real conversation.

How could you be successful and still feel like you do not belong in the room?

That is exactly the question Chapter 9 of Rock Your Business confronts head-on.

The chapter, titled How Could You Be Successful and Not Have It, was written by Samantha Frost, Caleb Hawkins, and Rafa Loyo. It goes straight at one of the least-discussed realities of scaling a company: the leaders driving the most growth are often carrying the heaviest load of self-doubt.

One thing the chapter makes clear is that imposter syndrome at the executive level is not about competence. It is about identity. As your company grows, your role changes faster than your internal self-image does. That gap is where the doubt lives.

Knowing that distinction changes how you lead through it.

Rock Your Business, by Jonathan Slain and Katherine Slain, available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
The most dangerous blind spot for $50M+ leaders is not a bad quarter. It is the absence of a life plan running alongside the business plan.

Most founders obsess over revenue milestones, headcount targets, and market share. Almost none build a clear picture of what they actually want their life to look like when the company hits $500M. A recent Entrepreneur.com piece confirmed this pattern: founders plan exhaustively for growth and almost never plan for what comes after.

Here is what that costs you:

First, major decisions get made reactively rather than by design. You sell, merge, or stay out of inertia, not intention.

Second, the business starts serving the owner's avoidance rather than the owner's goals. Growth becomes a way to delay the harder personal questions.

Third, the people closest to you, personally and professionally, pay the price for that ambiguity.

Life planning is not soft. It is the strategic work most leaders skip because it is uncomfortable, not because it is unimportant.

So here is the real question: If your business hit its goal tomorrow, would you know what to do next?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Entrepreneur.com made a point worth sitting with: founders pour enormous energy into growth planning and almost none into exit planning or life design.

At Autobahn Consultants, we see this consistently with companies scaling from $50M to $500M and beyond. The growth strategy is sharp. The personal roadmap is nonexistent.

This matters because at scale, the decisions get bigger and the personal cost of misalignment gets higher. Leaders who have not thought clearly about what they want beyond the next revenue target tend to make inconsistent decisions about people, capital, and culture.

Life planning is not a retirement conversation. It is a right-now leadership conversation.

If your business strategy does not have a personal counterpart, that is the gap worth closing first.

A piece in Entrepreneur.com recently highlighted something we have watched play out in boardrooms for years: founders build detailed plans for growth and almost nothing for the life waiting on the other side of it.

Chapter 10 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, tackles this directly. The chapter is called Coming Up for Air, and it was written by Samantha Frost alongside Jonathan and Katherine Slain.

The core idea: at a certain scale, the business will not run you into the ground. Your own unexamined assumptions about work and life will do that job instead.

The chapter introduces a framework for building a life plan that runs in parallel with your business plan, not after it, not eventually. Now.

There is one question in that chapter that stops most senior leaders cold. You will know it when you get there.
